stances.claim: The Comelec's deletion of 238,557 OFWs for failing to vote in two consecutive elections was legally and equitably flawed: the notice through two local newspapers and its website was 'miserably inadequate' for people living abroad, producing only 29 filings — proof that the procedure violated due process.
stances.rhetorical_move: adequacy-of-notice test: 29 filings out of 238,557 as statistical proof of procedural failure

stances.claim: Green card holders face a structurally coercive dilemma: the Comelec's affidavit of intent to return within three years exposes them to green card revocation and criminal prosecution, making the voting requirement a trap rather than an enabler — the ordinary rules for local voters cannot apply to them.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-trap argument: identifying the affidavit requirement as a legal catch-22 that suppresses rather than enables overseas participation

stances.claim: OFWs remit $21.4 billion annually — the single biggest source of foreign currency — and election laws should be construed liberally in their favor; the Philippines' economic wellbeing creates a reciprocal obligation to protect their political rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: economic-reciprocity argument: OFW economic contribution as a moral and policy basis for liberal construction of their voting rights

notable_anecdotes: Only 29 overseas Filipinos out of 238,557 delisted filing the required manifestation — CJ's 'only 29 — yes, only 29' double-emphasis making the inadequacy of the Comelec's notice viscerally unmistakable.

The green card affidavit trap: OFWs required to swear they will return within three years, then voting twice as evidence they never returned — creating a criminal self-incrimination scenario that CJ exposes as a structural deterrent embedded in the very mechanism meant to enable OFW participation.

Rodel Rodis citing Comelec Chair Brillantes' own September 29, 2011 promise not to cancel OFW registrations — a direct accountability move using the Comelec's own prior commitment against its subsequent action.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes the Comelec's March 5, 2013 reversal reinstating 238,557 overseas Filipino workers deleted from the National Registry of Overseas Absentee Voters for failing to vote in two consecutive elections (2007 and 2010). He identifies the procedural flaw: the Comelec's notice -- published in only two local newspapers and its website -- was 'miserably inadequate' for people living abroad, producing only 29 filings ('only 29 -- yes, only 29') out of 238,557 delisted voters, effectively denying due process. He catalogs structural barriers: sea-based workers who remitted $4.8 billion cannot vote at their 'original ports'; green card holders face a legal trap where the required affidavit of intent to return within three years risks green card revocation and criminal prosecution, and voting in two elections becomes incriminating evidence of non-return. CJ anchors his advocacy in SC precedents (Macalintal vs Comelec holding green card holders never lost their domicile of origin; Nicolas vs Comelec exempting dual citizens from the physical-return requirement) and in the OFWs' economic contribution: $21.4 billion in 2012 remittances, the single biggest source of foreign currency, creating a reciprocal obligation to 'construe election laws liberally in their favor.'
